question.:question/problem: What is the slope of the tangent line to the curve $y=18 x - 45 \cos{\left(x \right)}$ at the point $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope is the derivative evaluated at $x=\frac{\pi}{6}.$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sin x)=\cos x,$ and that $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\cos x)=-\sin x.$ Applying these formulas and the sum and constant multiple rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(18 x - 45 \cos{\left(x \right)}) \\ &= (45 \sin{\left(x \right)})+(18) \\ &= 45 \sin{\left(x \right)} + 18.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi}{6},$ we get

$$
y^{\prime}(\frac{\pi}{6})=18+45\sin(\frac{\pi}{6})=18+45\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{81}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the slope is $\frac{81}{2}.$

question.:question/problem: Calculate ${\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{54}}\sin{\left(18 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\,\text{d}x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=18 x + \frac{\pi}{3},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=18\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{18}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{54}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{2 \pi}{3}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{54}}\sin{\left(18 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\,\text{d}x &= {\int }_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}}1\sin(u)\cdot \frac{1}{18}\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{1}{18}{\int }_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}}\sin(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= - \frac{\cos{\left(u \right)}}{18}\big|_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}} \\ &= \frac{1}{36}-(- \frac{1}{36}) \\ &= \frac{1}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int 6 x \csc^{2}{\left(x^{2} \right)}\,\text{d}x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=x^{2},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2 x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6 x \csc^{2}{\left(x^{2} \right)}\,\text{d}x &= 3\int \csc^{2}{\left(u \right)}\,\text{d}u \\ &= - 3 \cot{\left(u \right)}+C \\ &= - 3 \cot{\left(x^{2} \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find ${f}^{'}(\frac{\pi }{6})$ if $f(x)=-15\operatorname{cot}x.$

Answer: {{answer}}

\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-15\operatorname{cot}x) \\  & =-15(-\csc^{2}x) \\  & =15\csc^{2}x\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{3}$ if $f(x)=11\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(11\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(11\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+{x}^{-1}) \\  & =11(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-11\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\sqrt{3}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) & =-11\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\sqrt{3})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =-11\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\sqrt{3})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(u)=\begin{bmatrix}\sin{\left(u \right)} \\ - e^{u} \\ u^{2}\end{bmatrix}$ and $u(t)=t^{2} + t - 1$, then $(f∘u)^{′}(t)=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the chain rule, we can write

$$
(f∘u)^{′}(t)=f′(u(t))u′(t)
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{′}(u) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}\left(\sin{\left(u \right)}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}\left(- e^{u}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}\left(u^{2}\right)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos{\left(u \right)} \\ - e^{u} \\ 2 u\end{bmatrix} \\ u^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(t^{2} + t - 1\right)=2 t + 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘u)^{′}(t) & =f′(u(t))u′(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\cos{\left(u(t) \right)} \\ - e^{u(t)} \\ 2 u(t)\end{bmatrix}\cdot \left(u^{′}(t)\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\cos{\left(t^{2} + t - 1 \right)} \\ - e^{t^{2} + t - 1} \\ 2 t^{2} + 2 t - 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \left(2 t + 1\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\left(2 t + 1\right) \cos{\left(t^{2} + t - 1 \right)} \\ \left(- 2 t - 1\right) e^{t^{2} + t - 1} \\ 2 \left(2 t + 1\right) \left(t^{2} + t - 1\right)\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
